world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Svelmoe, G. & T. Svelmoe 1974. Notes on Mansaka Grammar. SIL (phonology excerpt read on archive.org rosettaproject_msk_phon-1 covers phonemes/syllables but no stress statement)

new_statements.quote: Among the languages in Table 1, vowel length (or shortness) is clearly the most predominant feature at the word level. Stress is usually predictable (depending on the length or shortness of the penult vowel), or has a very low functional load [see below]. [...] Languages in Group E show only remnants of a pre-existing system of contrastive vowel length (Kalagan) or vowel shortness (Mansaka); stress plays no known role at the word level. In all Philippine languages stress or pitch accent is a syntactic feature, a means of indicating an accent group; it does not necessarily coincide with length.
new_statements.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1978. Proto-Philippine word accent: innovation or Proto-Hesperonesian retention? In S. A. Wurm & Lois Carrington (eds), Second International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics: Proceedings, Fascicle 1, 67-119. Pacific Linguistics C-61. Canberra: ANU.
new_statements.locator: p. 72 (PDF p. 6), §1.2 discussion of Table 1, Group E; preceding sentence on p. 71
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (pdfinfo title 'Proto-Philippine Word Accent: Innovation or Proto-Hesperonesian Retention?', author R. David Zorc) and re-extracted PDF p. 6 = printed p. 72 with extracted text; also checked the lines 259-291). Every clause of the quote is there verbatim (scanned letter-spacing only): p. 71 'Among the languages in Table 1, vowel length (or shortness) is clearly the most predominant feature at the word level. Stress is usually predictable (depending on the length or shortness of the penult vowel), or has a very low functional load [see below].' and p. 72 'Languages in Group E show only remnants of a pre-existing system of contrastive vowel length (Kalagan) or vowel shortnes…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Zorc, Mansaka has no known word-level stress. What survives of the Proto-Philippine accent system is a lexically distributed contrast of vowel shortness (Zorc 1978 Table 1 Group E: Mansaka lanut 'rice water' vs. lanŭt 'abaca'); Zorc 1977: 217 adds that Mansaka phonemic shortness corresponds to Bisayan ultima accent (Msk bayaw ~ Bs bayáw 'brother-in-law') but is only a remnant, since many forms reconstructible with accent are unmarked in Mansaka (mata 'eye', dilaq 'tongue'). The primary description (Svelmoe & Svelmoe 1974: 15 = 1990: xiii) says only: 'Vowel shortness is also phonemic... it has a low functional load' with minimal pairs (baga? 'lung' / băga? 'swelling'; butunga 'pull it' / bŭtung 'young coconut'; arigi 'post' / arĭgi 'shrimp fat'; tood 'purpose' / tŏod 'knee'), referring to Abrams 1963 for detail; it makes no statement about stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Zorc 1977: 217 notes many Mansaka forms are unmarked for accent where PCP accent is reconstructible; Zorc 1978: 105 n. 17 calls the retention of PPH short penult vowels in Mansaka 'sporadic' (bagaq 'boil', bayaw, gamut, gabi vs. unmarked mata, manuk).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Zorc explicitly 'at the word level'); Zorc treats stress/pitch accent in Philippine languages generally as a phrase-level (accent-group) feature. Svelmoe's vowel-shortness statement concerns lexical citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Mansaka proper (the Masara/upper Hijo/Maragusan Valley variety recorded by Svelmoe at Taytayan and Malamodao, Davao del Norte, 1954-73); Svelmoe 1974: 13-14 / 1990: xiii treat Mandaya and Mangaragan (Caraga Mandaya) as mutually intelligible dialects of the same group, and Zorc 1977 uses 'Boso-Caraga Mansakan'. Zorc's Group E data are labelled simply 'Mansaka'.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David Paul. 1977. The Bisayan dialects of the Philippines: subgrouping and reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44.
sources.note: p. 217 (§8.10): Mansaka and Kalagan exhibit 'a complementary phenomenon of phonemic shortness (in Mansaka) and phonemic length (in Kalagan) which coincides with Bs and Tg accent patterns. The phonemic shortness of Mansaka corresponds perfectly with accent on the ultima in Bs' (bayaw); 'these forms are only remnants of a pre-existing system since many forms are unmarked for accent'; p. 244-245: contrastive shortness in prefix yamă- 'able to'.
